title: Law in Global Affairs
description: The history of ideas, legal doctrines, institutional and administrative structures intended to organize and legalize international economic and political life, and recent efforts to rethink law's role.
optional_books: David Kennedy, A World of Struggle: How Power, Law, and Expertise Shape Global Political Economy (Princeton, 2016)
David Kennedy & Martti Koskenniemi, Of Law and the World: Critical Conversations on Power, History and Political Economy (Harvard, 2023)

deliverables.name: Paper 1 (500 words)
deliverables.due: Before the class discussing the chosen assignment; hard copy to Prof. Kennedy + email to Seamus Darby
deliverables.note: At least one paper must concern an assignment considered on or before Oct 19.

deliverables.name: Paper 2 (500 words)
deliverables.due: Before the class discussing the chosen assignment
deliverables.note: The two papers together are 1/3 of the grade.

deliverables.name: Final essay (2,000 words)
deliverables.due: Distributed on the last day of class; due on the last day of the exam period

relations_note: relation types: builds-on, extends, critiques, responds-to, applies, contrasts, illustrates, complicates, revisits

parts.title: The Mystery of Global Governance Today
The Background Architecture of Public International Law
New Thinking: Theories of the Whole
Global Governance in Action: War as an International Legal Institution

topics.title: The Disciplines of International Law and International Institutions – People with Projects and a History of Ideas
topics.overview: Opening frame: international law as a field made by *people with projects*, whose ideas have a history. Keep [[kennedy-chart]] at hand all semester — later topics slot into it.

topics.title: The Norms: Custom
topics.overview: Where does an unwritten norm come from? Start with [[icj-art38]], then watch how courts and scholars find (or construct) custom: [[paquete-habana]], [[lotus]], [[nuclear-weapons-ao]], against the process view of [[mcdougal-custom]].

topics.title: Sources – Normative Hierarchy and the Law/Non-law Boundary
topics.overview: Two questions run through this topic: is there a *hierarchy* among norms ([[jus-cogens]]), and where is the *edge* between law and non-law (unilateral declarations, twilight agreements, changed circumstances)?

topics.title: The Entities – Statehood and Sovereignty
topics.overview: Who counts as a state, and what does sovereignty actually give you? Note the syllabus says this may take two classes. Several cases here ([[schooner-exchange]], [[antelope]], [[american-banana]], [[corfu-1949]]) come back in Topic 10.

topics.title: Post-1945 Judicial Rulemaking
topics.overview: The ICJ as a maker of rules ([[nottebohm]], [[barcelona-traction]]) and its willingness to decide disputes that look political ([[tehran-hostages]], [[nicaragua-1984]]).

topics.title: The Entities: International Criminal Law – Individual Responsibility
topics.overview: The individual enters as a subject of international law. Readings range from the structural critique in [[koskenniemi-impunity]] to sovereigntist rejection in [[bolton-icc-2018]] and feminist critique in [[engle-grip]].

topics.title: The Powers: Jurisdiction
topics.overview: The three forms of jurisdiction and how far a state can reach beyond its territory. Doctrine ([[restatement-402-404]]) meets practice ([[bank-nova-scotia]]) and theory ([[malley-manas-nix]], [[berman-globalization-jurisdiction]]).

topics.title: The Powers: Territory
topics.overview: How title to territory is acquired and kept stable: effectivités ([[island-of-palmas]]), colonial ties and self-determination ([[western-sahara]]), uti possidetis ([[burkina-mali]]) — then the fantasy of an internationalised territory ([[berman-jerusalem]]).

topics.title: Mobilizing Architecture – Claims and State Responsibility
topics.overview: How the architecture is set in motion: attribution, breach, reparation, and self-help through countermeasures ([[ilc-arsiwa]], [[gabcikovo]], [[air-services]]).

topics.title: Before Modernity
topics.overview: Review from Topic 4: [[schooner-exchange]], [[antelope]], [[american-banana]], [[corfu-1949]]. Question: how do modern lawyers tell the story of their pre-modern predecessors, and what does the colonial encounter do to sovereignty ([[anghie-imperialism]])?

topics.title: The Turn to Modernism – 1914–1945
topics.overview: Interwar reinvention: new international law ([[alvarez-new-il]]), functionalism ([[jessup-functional]]), nationalities ([[redslob-nationalities]]) — and its dark mirror ([[vagts-third-reich]]).

topics.title: Modern International Law Extended and Contested – 1945–2000
subs: Moment 3 – Back to Norms and Values?
topics.overview: Three post-war moments: is international law *law* ([[austin-province]] vs [[kelsen-lecture-iii]])? law as policy for a hegemon ([[mcdougal-law-power]], [[jessup-transnational]], [[slaughter-around-un]])? and a return to norms ([[henkin-how-nations-behave]]).

topics.title: National Courts in a Transnational Legal Process and Questions of Reception
topics.overview: Koh's transnational legal process, then a stress test: the Trump years and the claimed end of the US-backed order.

topics.title: Consciousness – Political Economy
topics.overview: From ordoliberal blueprints ([[roepke-1955]]) to WTO legalism ([[bello-wto]]) and its Third World critique ([[shalakany-arbitration]]).

topics.title: Changing Consciousness as a Governance Strategy – Human Rights and Environmental Protection
topics.overview: Human rights and environmental law as attempts to change how people think, with their dark sides ([[kennedy-hr-problem]]). Environmental readings are recommended.

topics.title: Institutions as “Governance”
subs: League of Nations, the United Nations, and a History of Reform
Leadership as Governance – The Secretary General
topics.overview: Institutions as myth ([[barthes-eiffel]]), as reform project, as leadership ([[kennedy-sg]]), and as administration ([[kingsbury-gal]]).

topics.title: Regulation and Private Ordering
topics.overview: Governance by corporations, value chains and tech platforms: who legislates when the state is not the main actor?

topics.title: Systems Theory and Fragmentation
topics.overview: Is international law one system or many colliding regimes? ILC vs [[fischer-lescano-teubner]] vs [[lang-regimes]]; then capitalism's legal infrastructure ([[koskenniemi-laws-rule-us]]).

topics.title: Global Hierarchies
topics.overview: Hierarchy as a structure of the whole: colonialism and its rhetoric, then Third World resistance (NIEO, social movements, TWAIL).

topics.title: New Geographies – The Turn to the Local
topics.overview: International law lived in local spaces and cities.

topics.title: “The Law of Armed Conflict,” “Humanitarian Law,” the “Laws of War,” or “jus in bello”
topics.overview: The law in war, its history and weapons law, and the psychology and language of those who plan war ([[freud-war-death]], [[cohn-sex-death]]).

topics.title: The Law of Force and the Use of Force – Modern War and Modern Law
topics.overview: War as politics ([[clausewitz-on-war]]), power as discipline ([[foucault-body]]), and law as the vocabulary of modern war ([[kennedy-legal-expertise-war]]).

readings.author: Damrosch & Murphy
readings.title: Introduction to the Study of International Law

readings.author: Nathaniel Berman
readings.title: Modernism, Nationalism, and the Rhetoric of Reconstruction
readings.tldr: Reads interwar international law as a *modernist* project: a self-conscious reconstruction of the discipline that tried to channel nationalist passion through new legal forms.

readings.author: David Kennedy
readings.title: Chart: Intellectual History
readings.tldr: Kennedy's map of the field's intellectual history. A reference frame for the whole course.

readings.author: ICJ Statute
readings.title: Statute of the International Court of Justice, art. 38
readings.tldr: The canonical list of sources: treaties, custom (general practice accepted as law), general principles; judicial decisions and teachings as subsidiary means.

readings.author: Oscar Schachter
readings.title: International Law in Theory and Practice (excerpts on custom)

readings.author: U.S. Supreme Court
readings.title: The Paquete Habana
readings.tldr: Coastal fishing boats are exempt from capture as prize under customary international law, found in centuries of practice and in treatises. "International law is part of our law" where no treaty or controlling act decides.

readings.author: Damrosch & Murphy
readings.title: Customary Law Questions

readings.author: International Law Commission
readings.title: Draft Conclusions on Identification of Customary International Law
readings.tldr: Two elements, each to be shown separately: a general practice, and acceptance as law (opinio juris). Also covers the persistent objector rule.

readings.author: Myres S. McDougal
readings.title: McDougal on Customary Law
readings.tldr: Custom as an ongoing process of claim and response: decision-makers accept or reject states' unilateral claims, rather than applying a fixed rule.

readings.author: PCIJ
readings.title: The Case of the S.S. “Lotus” (France v. Turkey)
readings.tldr: Turkey may prosecute the French officer after a high-seas collision. Limits on state independence cannot be presumed: states are free unless a prohibiting rule exists. Not prosecuting in the past is not evidence of opinio juris.

readings.author: ICJ
readings.title: Legality of the Threat or Use of Nuclear Weapons (Advisory Opinion)
readings.tldr: Neither custom nor treaty clearly authorises or bans nuclear weapons. Their use would generally breach humanitarian law, but the Court cannot decide the extreme case of self-defence where a state's survival is at stake. A famous *non liquet* (no clear answer).

readings.author: Oscar Schachter
readings.title: International Law in Theory and Practice (excerpts on general principles)

readings.author: International Law Commission
readings.title: Fragmentation of International Law (excerpts on jus cogens)
readings.tldr: Jus cogens, erga omnes obligations and UN Charter art. 103 as the few tools that create hierarchy in an otherwise flat system.

readings.author: Hilary Charlesworth & Christine Chinkin
readings.title: The Gender of Jus Cogens
readings.tldr: The supposedly universal peremptory norms reflect male experience. They target public, state-inflicted harms and leave out harms women typically suffer in the 'private' sphere.

readings.author: ICJ
readings.title: Nuclear Tests Case (Australia v. France)
readings.tldr: France's public statements that it would stop atmospheric testing created a binding legal obligation. A public declaration made with intent to be bound is law, so Australia's claim no longer had an object.

readings.author: Oscar Schachter
readings.title: The Twilight Existence of Nonbinding International Agreements
readings.tldr: Gentlemen's agreements and political accords (e.g. the Helsinki Final Act) are not legally binding, yet they carry real political and moral weight and shape conduct.

readings.author: VCLT
readings.title: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, arts. 61–62
readings.tldr: Narrow exits from treaties: supervening impossibility (art. 61) and fundamental change of circumstances, *rebus sic stantibus* (art. 62).

readings.author: N.Y. Court of Appeals (Cardozo)
readings.title: Techt v. Hughes
readings.tldr: Did WWI end a US–Prussia treaty that let aliens inherit land? Cardozo: provisions compatible with war survive it, so the inheritance right stood.

readings.author: Oliver J. Lissitzyn
readings.title: The International Load Line Convention Case
readings.tldr: On the 1941 US claim that changed circumstances (wartime) let it suspend the 1930 Load Line Convention.

readings.author: Damrosch & Murphy
readings.title: States

readings.author: Montevideo Convention
readings.title: Convention on the Rights and Duties of States, arts. 1–3
readings.tldr: Four criteria for statehood: permanent population, defined territory, government, capacity for relations. Art. 3: a state exists politically regardless of recognition.

readings.author: Arnulf Becker Lorca
readings.title: Mestizo International Law: A Global Intellectual History 1842–1933
readings.tldr: Jurists from the semi-periphery appropriated classical European international law to claim sovereign equality. The result was a *mestizo* (mixed) international law, not one simply imposed from the centre.

readings.author: Schwirtz, Varenikova & Gladstone
readings.title: Putin Calls Ukrainian Statehood a Fiction. History Suggests Otherwise.

readings.author: Tracy Robinson
readings.title: Dyadic Caribbean Constitutions

readings.author: N.Y. Court of Appeals
readings.title: Salimoff & Co. v. Standard Oil Co.
readings.tldr: The US had not recognised the USSR, but the court still treated Soviet confiscation decrees as acts of a real (de facto) government. Facts on the ground beat the formality of recognition.

readings.author: Tacey Rychter
readings.title: New Emoji is a Meaningful Symbol for Indigenous Australians

readings.author: U.S. Supreme Court (Marshall)
readings.title: The Schooner Exchange v. McFaddon
readings.tldr: A state's jurisdiction in its territory is exclusive and absolute. Yet by implied consent it waives jurisdiction over a foreign sovereign's warship, so the French vessel is immune.

readings.author: U.S. Supreme Court (Marshall)
readings.title: The Antelope
readings.tldr: The slave trade is contrary to natural law, but not to the law of nations, because nations practised it. A stark positivist result, decided over the claims of the enslaved Africans.

readings.author: Henry Maine
readings.title: The Kathiawar States and Sovereignty
readings.tldr: Sovereignty is divisible: the Kathiawar chiefs kept some sovereign powers under British paramountcy.

readings.author: U.S. Supreme Court (Holmes)
readings.title: American Banana Co. v. United Fruit Co.
readings.tldr: The Sherman Act does not reach conduct in Panama and Costa Rica. Whether an act is lawful depends on the law of the place where it was done: strict territoriality.

readings.author: Morris R. Cohen
readings.title: Property and Sovereignty
readings.tldr: Property is a form of sovereignty: private ownership (*dominium*) gives power over other people (*imperium*). The public/private line is a political choice.

readings.author: ICJ
readings.title: Corfu Channel Case (United Kingdom v. Albania)
readings.tldr: Albania is responsible for mines that damaged British warships: every state must not knowingly let its territory be used against others' rights. The UK's later minesweeping violated Albanian sovereignty.

readings.author: Karen Knop
readings.title: Re/Statements: Feminism and State Sovereignty in International Law

readings.author: Damrosch & Murphy
readings.title: Acquisition and Denial of Nationality

readings.author: ICJ
readings.title: Nottebohm Case (Liechtenstein v. Guatemala)
readings.tldr: Liechtenstein cannot protect Nottebohm against Guatemala: his naturalisation lacked a *genuine connection* with Liechtenstein. Nationality on the international plane requires an effective link.

readings.author: ICJ
readings.title: Barcelona Traction, Light and Power Co. (Belgium v. Spain)
readings.tldr: Belgium cannot protect the shareholders of a Canadian company; the state of incorporation is the one that can. Famous dictum: some obligations are owed *erga omnes*, to the international community as a whole.

readings.author: ICJ
readings.title: United States Diplomatic and Consular Staff in Tehran (Order of Dec. 15)
readings.tldr: Provisional measures ordering the hostages' release. A dispute's political side does not stop the Court from ruling on its legal side.

readings.author: ICJ
readings.title: Military and Paramilitary Activities in and against Nicaragua (Jurisdiction)
readings.tldr: The Court takes jurisdiction despite the US attempt to withdraw. It rejects the argument that an ongoing armed conflict belongs only to the Security Council and politics.

readings.author: Martti Koskenniemi
readings.title: Between Impunity and Show Trials
readings.tldr: International criminal trials are caught between impunity and show trials. The courtroom becomes a stage for competing histories (e.g. Milošević), so ICL cannot escape the politics of truth.

readings.author: John Bolton
readings.title: Protecting American Constitutionalism and Sovereignty from International Threats
readings.tldr: The US national security adviser attacks the ICC as an illegitimate threat to US sovereignty and threatens sanctions on its officials.

readings.author: Zinaida Miller
readings.title: Times of Violence, Times of Justice

readings.author: Tor Krever
readings.title: Scurrying to the Hague

readings.author: Mark A. Drumbl
readings.title: Smouldering Semantics

readings.author: Karen Engle
readings.title: Introduction, The Grip of Sexual Violence in Conflict
readings.tldr: How sexual violence in conflict came to dominate feminist engagement with international law. A focus on criminalisation narrowed the wider agenda.

readings.author: Damrosch & Murphy
readings.title: Three Forms of Jurisdiction
readings.tldr: Jurisdiction to prescribe, to adjudicate, and to enforce.

readings.author: American Law Institute
readings.title: Restatement (Third) of Foreign Relations Law §§402–404
readings.tldr: Bases for jurisdiction (territory, effects, nationality, protective principle), a reasonableness test (§403), and universal jurisdiction (§404).

readings.author: 11th Cir.
readings.title: United States v. Bank of Nova Scotia
readings.tldr: A US grand jury subpoena is enforced against a Canadian bank's Miami branch for records held in the Bahamas, despite Bahamian bank secrecy law.

readings.author: Anna Sauerbrey
readings.title: The Failure of Europe's Feeble Muscle Flexing

readings.author: Malley, Manas & Nix
readings.title: Constructing the State Extraterritorially
readings.tldr: Jurisdictional argument does not just divide competence among states that already exist. It constructs the state itself, its 'national interest', and transnational norms.

readings.author: Paul Schiff Berman
readings.title: The Globalization of Jurisdiction
readings.tldr: Proposes a cosmopolitan, pluralist view of jurisdiction, based on community affiliations that do not stop at territorial borders.

readings.author: Shahd Hammouri
readings.title: Shipments of Death

readings.author: Permanent Court of Arbitration (Huber)
readings.title: Island of Palmas (United States v. The Netherlands)
readings.tldr: Title requires the continuous and peaceful display of state authority. Discovery gives only an inchoate (incomplete) title. Also introduces the intertemporal law.

readings.author: ICJ
readings.title: Western Sahara (Advisory Opinion)
readings.tldr: The territory was not *terra nullius* when Spain colonised it. Morocco and the Mauritanian entity had legal ties to it, but not territorial sovereignty, and those ties do not override self-determination.

readings.author: Richard Pérez-Peña
readings.title: How a Long Insurgency Plays into Trump's Move on Morocco

readings.author: ICJ
readings.title: Frontier Dispute (Burkina Faso v. Mali)
readings.tldr: *Uti possidetis juris* is a general principle: colonial administrative boundaries become international borders at independence, for the sake of stability.

readings.author: Jure Vidmar
readings.title: Greenland and Territorial Acquisition under International Law

readings.author: Nathaniel Berman
readings.title: Legalizing Jerusalem, or, Of Law, Fantasy, and Faith

readings.author: Damrosch & Murphy
readings.title: Rules on State Responsibility

readings.author: International Law Commission
readings.title: Draft Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts
readings.tldr: A wrongful act is conduct attributable to a state that breaches an obligation. Consequences: cessation and reparation. Also lists the circumstances that preclude wrongfulness (consent, self-defence, countermeasures, necessity…).

readings.author: Damrosch & Murphy
readings.title: Countermeasures

readings.author: ICJ
readings.title: Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros Project (Hungary v. Slovakia)
readings.tldr: Hungary's plea of ecological necessity fails. Slovakia's 'Variant C' is a disproportionate countermeasure. The 1977 treaty survives, and both sides must negotiate.

readings.author: Arbitral Tribunal
readings.title: Air Services Agreement Case (France v. United States)
readings.tldr: The US could suspend Air France flights to Los Angeles as a proportionate countermeasure to France's breach: self-help in a decentralised system.

readings.author: Lillich & Paxman
readings.title: State Responsibility for Injuries to Aliens Occasioned by Terrorist Activities

readings.author: The New York Times
readings.title: The Urgent Search for a Cyber Bullet Against Iran

readings.author: David Kennedy
readings.title: Primitive Legal Scholarship
readings.tldr: Reads Vitoria, Suárez, Gentili and Grotius not as crude forerunners but as working within a different structure of authority. Shows how modern scholarship builds its own story of progress.

readings.author: Annelise Riles
readings.title: Aspiration and Control: International Legal Rhetoric and the Essentialization of Culture

readings.author: Antony Anghie
readings.title: Imperialism, Sovereignty and the Making of International Law
readings.tldr: The 'dynamic of difference': 19th-century positivism split the world into civilised and uncivilised. Sovereignty itself was formed in the colonial encounter, not merely extended to it.

readings.author: Alejandro Alvarez
readings.title: The New International Law
readings.tldr: A Latin American call for a *new* international law built on interdependence and social solidarity, with room for regional (American) international law.

readings.author: Philip Jessup
readings.title: The Functional Approach as Applied to International Law
readings.cite: Third Conference of Teachers of International Law 1

readings.author: Robert Redslob
readings.title: The Problem of Nationalities

readings.author: Detlev Vagts
readings.title: International Law in the Third Reich
readings.tldr: How Nazi-era international lawyers reworked the discipline (Großraum ideas, völkisch theories) and how the profession went along with it.

readings.author: John Austin
readings.title: The Province of Jurisprudence Determined
readings.tldr: Law is the command of a sovereign backed by a sanction. Since no sovereign stands above states, international law is only 'positive morality'.

readings.author: Hans Kelsen
readings.title: Lecture III: International Law and the State
readings.cite: Law and Peace in International Relations, 56 (excerpts)
readings.tldr: International law *is* law: it has sanctions, applied in a decentralised way (reprisals, war). Monism: national and international law form one system.

readings.author: ICJ
readings.title: Corfu Channel Case (merits), revisited
readings.tldr: Reread for its grounds: Albania's duty to warn rests on 'elementary considerations of humanity', a source of obligation outside treaties.

readings.author: Myres McDougal
readings.title: Law and Power
readings.tldr: Rejects rules-as-formalism: law is a process of authoritative decision serving values (human dignity, and in practice the free world's interests). This is the New Haven school.

readings.author: Oscar Schachter
readings.title: Dag Hammarskjold and the Relation of Law to Politics

readings.author: Philip Jessup
readings.title: Transnational Law
readings.tldr: 'Transnational law': all law that regulates actions or events crossing national borders, public and private, beyond the old categories.

readings.author: Ruth Wedgwood
readings.title: Unilateral Action in a Multilateral World

readings.author: Anne-Marie Slaughter
readings.title: Good Reasons for Going Around the U.N.
readings.tldr: On the eve of the Iraq war: acting without Security Council authorisation could be legitimate even if not strictly legal.

readings.sub: Moment 3 – Back to Norms and Values?
readings.author: Louis Henkin
readings.title: How Nations Behave: Law and Foreign Policy
readings.tldr: "Almost all nations observe almost all principles of international law and almost all of their obligations almost all of the time." International law works mostly through routine compliance, not enforcement.

readings.sub: Moment 3 – Back to Norms and Values?
readings.author: Louis Henkin
readings.title: International Law and the Inter-State System

readings.author: Harold H. Koh
readings.title: Transnational Legal Process
readings.tldr: Compliance happens through *interaction, interpretation, internalisation*: norms seep into domestic law and institutions through repeated transnational contact.

readings.author: Harold H. Koh
readings.title: The Trump Administration and International Law
readings.tldr: Transnational legal process as resistance: courts, states, cities, NGOs and bureaucracies push back against a disruptive executive.

readings.author: Jack Goldsmith & Shannon Togawa Mercer
readings.title: International Law and Institutions in the Trump Era

readings.author: Eyal Benvenisti
readings.title: The Resilience of International Law in the Face of Empire

readings.author: Monica Hakimi & Jacob Katz Cogan
readings.title: The End of the U.S.-Backed International Order and the Future of International Law

readings.author: Wilhelm Röpke
readings.title: Economic Order and International Law
readings.tldr: Ordoliberal blueprint: a liberal international economy needs a legal framework that protects markets and property from national politics.

readings.author: Judith Bello
readings.title: The WTO Dispute Settlement Understanding: Less is More
readings.tldr: WTO rules work precisely because they are *not* binding in the classic sense: a losing state can comply or pay through rebalanced concessions.

readings.author: Amr A. Shalakany
readings.title: Arbitration and the Third World: A Plea for Reassessing Bias Under the Specter of Neoliberalism
readings.tldr: Bias in international arbitration against Third World parties should be rethought: it is built into neoliberal legal ideas, not just a matter of individual partiality.

readings.author: Damrosch & Murphy
readings.title: Foundations of Human Rights in Law

readings.author: Damrosch & Murphy
readings.title: Competing Interests

readings.author: Walter Johnson
readings.title: To Remake the World: Slavery, Racial Capitalism, and Justice
readings.tldr: Slavery as the foundation of *racial capitalism*, not a premodern exception to it. This has consequences for what 'justice' can mean today.

readings.author: David Kennedy
readings.title: The International Human Rights Movement: Part of the Problem?
readings.tldr: A list of the movement's possible costs: it takes up the whole emancipatory imagination, centres the state, treats harms as violations rather than structures, and legitimates the order it criticises.

readings.author: Vasuki Nesiah
readings.title: Slavery's Afterlives: Humanitarian Imperialism and Free Contract

readings.author: David Kennedy
readings.title: Spring Break: The Activist Individual (recommended)

readings.author: Philippe Sands
readings.title: Greening International Law, Parts Two & Three (recommended)

readings.author: Richard Falk
readings.title: Environmental Protection in an Era of Globalization (recommended)

readings.author: Haroon Siddique
readings.title: Legal Experts Worldwide Draw up 'Historic' Definition of Ecocide (recommended)

readings.author: Burgis-Kasthala & Masetti Placci
readings.title: Lost for Words, yet Grasping for Neologisms: Gaza, Genocide and the Discursive Limits of International Law

readings.author: Roland Barthes
readings.title: The Eiffel Tower
readings.cite: The Eiffel Tower and Other Mythologies, 3

readings.sub: League of Nations, the United Nations, and a History of Reform
readings.author: P.E. Corbett
readings.title: What is the League of Nations?

readings.sub: Leadership as Governance – The Secretary General
readings.author: David Kennedy
readings.title: Leader, Clerk or Policy Entrepreneur? The Secretary-General in a Complex World

readings.author: Kingsbury, Krisch & Stewart
readings.title: The Emergence of Global Administrative Law
readings.tldr: Much global governance is really *administration*. A 'global administrative space' is emerging, held to norms of transparency, participation, reasoned decision and review.

readings.author: Zinaida Miller
readings.title: Perils of Parity: Palestine's Permanent Transition

readings.author: Dan Danielsen
readings.title: Corporate Power and Global Order
readings.tldr: Corporations are not just objects of regulation: they shape global order, and the rules of corporate law are themselves a form of global governance.

readings.author: Dan Danielsen
readings.title: Local Rules and a Global Economy: An Economic Policy Perspective

readings.author: Adam Satariano
readings.title: The World's Tech Ambassador to the Tech Industry

readings.author: IGLP Law and Global Production Working Group
readings.title: The Role of Law in Global Value Chains: A Research Manifesto
readings.tldr: Law structures global value chains: it shapes who captures value and power along the chain. A research agenda for seeing law where economists see markets.

readings.author: The New York Times
readings.title: Elon Musk's Unmatched Power in the Stars

readings.author: International Law Commission
readings.title: Fragmentation as a Phenomenon
readings.tldr: Specialised regimes (trade, human rights, environment…) have multiplied, each with its own logic. The ILC answers with lawyerly tools of coordination: lex specialis, systemic integration.

readings.author: Fischer-Lescano & Teubner
readings.title: Regime-Collisions: The Vain Search for Legal Unity in the Fragmentation of Global Law
readings.tldr: Fragmentation mirrors collisions between sectors of world society. Legal unity is impossible; at most, a loose compatibility between regimes.

readings.author: Andrew T.F. Lang
readings.title: Legal Regimes and Professional Knowledges: The Internal Politics of Regime Definition
readings.tldr: Regimes are not given: they are defined by professional knowledge and expert practice, and that definitional work is political.

readings.author: Martti Koskenniemi
readings.title: The Laws That Rule Us: The Legal Infrastructure of Global Capitalism

readings.author: Elena Chachko & J. Benton Heath
readings.title: A Watershed Moment for Sanctions? Russia, Ukraine and the Economic Battlefield

readings.author: Nnamdi Azikiwe
readings.title: Liberian Diplomacy

concepts.name: Sources of international law
concepts.short: Where binding norms come from: treaties, custom, general principles (ICJ Statute art. 38).

concepts.name: Customary international law
concepts.short: Unwritten law from general state practice plus opinio juris (acceptance as law).

concepts.name: General principles of law
concepts.short: Principles common to legal systems, or basic to the international order, filling gaps.

concepts.name: Jus cogens
concepts.short: Peremptory norms from which no derogation is permitted; the top of a claimed normative hierarchy.

concepts.name: Obligations erga omnes
concepts.short: Obligations owed to the international community as a whole (Barcelona Traction dictum).

concepts.name: The law / non-law boundary
concepts.short: Where law ends and politics, morality or mere commitment begin; a recurring question.

concepts.name: Soft law & non-binding agreements
concepts.short: Commitments that shape conduct without legal bindingness.

concepts.name: Unilateral declarations
concepts.short: Public statements that bind a state if made with intent to be bound.

concepts.name: Rebus sic stantibus / changed circumstances
concepts.short: Terminating or suspending treaties because circumstances changed fundamentally or performance became impossible.

concepts.name: Statehood
concepts.short: What makes an entity a state (Montevideo criteria) and who decides.

concepts.name: Recognition
concepts.short: Declaratory vs constitutive views: does recognition create a state or merely acknowledge one?

concepts.name: Sovereignty
concepts.short: The bundle of rights and powers of states; absolute or relative, divisible or not.

concepts.name: Territoriality
concepts.short: The principle that law and power stop at a state's territory.

concepts.name: Jurisdiction
concepts.short: Power to prescribe, adjudicate and enforce law.

concepts.name: Extraterritoriality
concepts.short: Reaching conduct abroad: effects doctrine, nationality, secondary sanctions.

concepts.name: Territory & title
concepts.short: How territory is acquired and held: effective occupation, cession, uti possidetis.

concepts.name: Uti possidetis juris
concepts.short: Colonial administrative lines become international borders at independence.

concepts.name: Self-determination
concepts.short: Peoples' right to decide their political status; in tension with territorial stability.

concepts.name: Nationality & diplomatic protection
concepts.short: Who a state may protect internationally, and the 'genuine link' requirement.

concepts.name: Judicial rulemaking
concepts.short: International courts creating doctrine while claiming to apply it.

concepts.name: Adjudicating political questions
concepts.short: Whether courts can or should decide disputes that look political.

concepts.name: Individual criminal responsibility
concepts.short: Individuals, not just states, answerable under international law (ICL).

concepts.name: State responsibility
concepts.short: Attribution + breach = internationally wrongful act, leading to cessation and reparation.

concepts.name: Countermeasures & sanctions
concepts.short: Lawful self-help against a wrongdoing state, if proportionate.

concepts.name: Positivism
concepts.short: Law is what states consent to or what a sovereign commands, separate from morality.

concepts.name: Naturalism
concepts.short: Law grounded in reason, nature or divine order, prior to state will.

concepts.name: Interwar modernism
concepts.short: 1914–45 reinvention of international law: institutions, nationalities, functionalism, new forms.

concepts.name: Functionalism / pragmatism
concepts.short: Judging law by what it does, not by formal categories.

concepts.name: New Haven policy science
concepts.short: McDougal's view: law as a process of authoritative decision in pursuit of values.

concepts.name: Law and politics
concepts.short: How law relates to power, interest and policy; the field's master question.

concepts.name: Compliance
concepts.short: Why and when states obey international law.

concepts.name: Transnational legal process
concepts.short: Koh: interaction, interpretation, internalisation of norms across borders.

concepts.name: Reception in national courts
concepts.short: How domestic courts absorb and apply international law.

concepts.name: Political economy
concepts.short: Law's role in distributing economic power and wealth globally.

concepts.name: Public / private distinction
concepts.short: The line between state and market, family and politics, which critics show is contestable.

concepts.name: Private ordering
concepts.short: Governance by corporations, contracts, value chains and platforms.

concepts.name: Human rights
concepts.short: Rights-based governance strategy and its critiques.

concepts.name: Dark sides of virtue
concepts.short: Kennedy: humanitarian projects can produce costs and blind spots.

concepts.name: Environmental protection
concepts.short: Greening international law: principles, techniques, ecocide.

concepts.name: International institutions
concepts.short: League, UN, Secretary-General: institutions as governance and myth.

concepts.name: Global administrative law
concepts.short: Accountability norms for global administrative bodies.

concepts.name: Fragmentation
concepts.short: Proliferation of specialised regimes and the (im)possibility of unity.

concepts.name: Colonialism & hierarchy
concepts.short: How empire shaped sovereignty, civilisation and international law's categories.

concepts.name: TWAIL & Third World resistance
concepts.short: Third World Approaches to International Law; NIEO; law from below.

concepts.name: The local & the city
concepts.short: International law lived in local spaces, cities and communities.

concepts.name: Jus in bello (IHL)
concepts.short: The law governing the conduct of war.

concepts.name: Jus ad bellum
concepts.short: The law on resort to force: UN Charter art. 2(4), self-defence, Security Council authorisation.

concepts.name: Feminist critique
concepts.short: Gendered assumptions in international law's categories.

concepts.name: People with projects / expertise
concepts.short: Kennedy: the field as made by professionals and their projects; expertise as power.

connections.note: The 1996 opinion reopens the Lotus question: if no rule prohibits nuclear weapons, are states simply free? The Court refuses to say so clearly.
Custom as an ongoing process of claim and response vs. the ILC's tidy two-element test.
The same policy-science method, now a full theory of law as authoritative decision.
A court actually *finding* custom from practice and writers, as art. 38 describes.
A unilateral statement becomes binding, while negotiated non-binding agreements stay in the twilight. Intent to be bound decides.
Changed circumstances (war) and treaty survival, before the VCLT codified it.
Rebus sic stantibus invoked by a state in practice.
The ILC's hierarchy of 'universal' norms rests on a gendered public/private split.
Without recognition, a de facto government still counts: facts vs. formalities.
Montevideo (1933) as itself a product of semi-peripheral lawyers' strategy.
Strict territoriality, from exclusive jurisdiction at home to no jurisdiction abroad.
From Holmes' strict territoriality to aggressive extraterritorial enforcement.
The Restatement's neutral 'bases' of jurisdiction hide how jurisdiction constructs state interest.
Private property abroad (United Fruit) is itself a form of sovereign power.
Private power as public governance, updated for global corporations.
Divisible, colonial sovereignty vs. Marshall's exclusive and absolute territorial sovereignty.
Positivism's acceptance of slavery as a practice of 'nations' shows the dynamic of difference.
Genuine link for individuals vs. formal state of incorporation for companies.
Both reject the idea that a political or armed dispute is beyond the Court.
Stability of colonial borders (uti possidetis) vs. self-determination of peoples.
Effective control is not the whole story: pre-colonial social and political ties count.
The 2020 US recognition of Moroccan sovereignty against the ICJ's 1975 opinion.
Classic modes of acquiring territory tested against a contemporary claim.
Necessity and countermeasures from the Articles applied, and rejected, in practice.
Proportionate countermeasures as self-help.
Same case, reread: Topic 4 for sovereignty, Topic 12 for the source of obligation.
How the discipline narrates its pre-modern past.
From historical diagnosis to a programme for postcolonial international law.
1928 functionalism grows into 1956 'transnational law'.
Answers Austin: international law has sanctions too, just decentralised.
Rejects rule-centred formalism for policy and process.
Back to rules and compliance after policy-science.
Legitimate unilateralism outside the UN.
Explains *why* nations mostly comply: internalisation.
The process theory as resistance strategy.
Less rupture, more continuity than Koh suggests.
End of an order vs. resilience of the law.
Insulating trade from politics through legal design.
Neoliberal legalism and bias against the Third World.
Slavery's legacy in humanitarianism and free contract.
A humanitarian project and its dark sides.
Governance as administration with accountability vs. as leadership and entrepreneurship.
No unity is possible, only collision management.
Regimes are made by professional knowledge, not given by social sectors.
Same ILC report: hierarchy (Topic 3) and fragmentation (Topic 18).
From the politics of trials to the legal infrastructure of capitalism.
Using sovereignty and law against the economic order colonialism built.
Resistance from social movements, not just Third World states.
A TWAIL critique of contemporary approaches.
From semi-peripheral appropriation of sovereignty to bargaining over inequality.
Knop re-looks at who and what sovereignty hides: women, then cities.
Modernist legal imagination applied to an internationalised city.
Psychology of war, now through gender and expert language.
Law becomes one of the 'other means' of politics in war.
Diffuse, technical power: law as discipline of violence.
Sovereigntist rejection vs. structural critique of international criminal justice.
Feminist success in criminalising sexual violence and its narrowing effects.
From bilateral countermeasures to economic warfare by sanctions.

themes.name: Sovereignty: absolute, divided, relative
themes.description: Follow how sovereignty is asserted, divided, limited and re-asserted across the course.

themes.name: Where does law end?
themes.description: Custom, twilight agreements, declarations, Austin vs Kelsen, WTO 'less is more': the course keeps returning to the boundary of law.

themes.name: Empire, colonialism and hierarchy
themes.description: Who was inside and outside the 'family of nations', and how that shaped the law's basic categories.

themes.name: Law and the global economy
themes.description: Property as sovereignty, ordoliberal design, WTO, value chains, sanctions: law distributes economic power.

themes.name: Feminist critique
themes.description: The gendered public/private divide, from jus cogens to sovereignty to the language of war.

themes.name: People with projects: expertise and its dark sides
themes.description: Kennedy's through-line: international law as professional practice, with costs that its practitioners don't see.
